findings.printedLatin: Non enim invenitur orare in hoc cantico, nisi per duo verba tantum, ut dicit: « Laetata sum in salutari meo, » et aliud est, « quia non est Deus praeter te. »
findings.englishAsRendered: For she is not found to pray in this canticle except by two phrases only, when she says: « I have rejoiced in thy salvation, » and the other, « because there is no God beside thee. »
findings.conjecture: Migne prints *in salutari MEO*; our English silently prints "thy salvation." Either the plate is defective (Vulgate 1 Reg. 2:1 *in salutari tuo*) and must be rendered "my salvation" with a crux, or the conformation must go. It cannot be repaired inside the translation.
findings.whyContradiction: Twelve lines later Migne prints the SAME verse as the lemma « Quia laetata sum in salutari TUO », and our English gives "in thy salvation" there too — so two printed readings that differ (meo / tuo) have been levelled into one English. Worse, the argument turns on the difference: Rabanus is counting which words in the canticle are actually PRAYER, i.e. second-person address to God; the paired instance he adduces is « quia non est Deus praeter TE ». Rendering *meo* as "thy" pre-supplies the very second person the passage is testing for.

findings.printedLatin: « Sapientia aedificavit sibi domum et suffulsit columnas septem [n: (Prov. IX)]. »
findings.englishAsRendered: « Wisdom hath built herself a house, and hath hewn out seven pillars [n: (Prov. IX)]. »
findings.conjecture: *suffulsit* = "propped up / underpinned"; "hewn out" renders the Vulgate's *excidit*, a word not on this plate. Read "and hath propped up seven pillars."
findings.whyContradiction: The remembered Douay wording has displaced the printed verb outright — the English contains a word (*excidit*) Migne does not print, in a proof-text adduced for the SEVEN (the number is the whole point of the citation: 'agnoscentibus numerum septenarium, quo est universa Ecclesiae significata protectio'), so the lemma is doing load-bearing work and must be the lemma actually printed.

findings.printedLatin: « Suscitat a terra PAUPEREM » … « Et de stercore erigit INOPEM. »
findings.englishAsRendered: « He raiseth up the NEEDY from the earth » … « And out of the dunghill he lifteth up the POOR. »
findings.conjecture: Migne prints *pauperem* with *a terra* and *inopem* with *de stercore*; the Douay of 1 Reg. 2:8 has the reverse pairing ("the needy from the dust… the poor from the dunghill"), and our English has taken the Douay pairing over the printed one. Read "He raiseth up the POOR MAN from the earth" / "out of the dunghill he lifteth up the NEEDY."
findings.whyContradiction: Our own English at the close of the same paragraph, translating Migne's own recapitulation *De terra ergo suscitatus est, ille supra omnes divites PAUPER erectus est, et de illo stercore super omnes opulentos ille INOPS*, renders it "that POOR man lifted up above all the rich, and out of that dunghill … that NEEDY one" — the exact opposite binding to the one our lemmata give four lines earlier. One of the two must be wrong, and it is the lemmata, because they are the ones that disagree with the plate.

findings.printedLatin: filiis vero Israel, quibus profuit, quod aqua divisa est, non fuit ille spiritus irae Dei?
findings.englishAsRendered: but to the children of Israel, whom it profited that the water was divided — was that not the spirit of God's wrath?
findings.conjecture: The clause is a flat denial, not a rhetorical question: "but to the children of Israel, whom it profited that the water was divided, that was NOT the spirit of God's wrath." (Migne's terminal '?' is punctuation, not argument.) Turning it into a rhetorical question converts a printed negative into an assertion of exactly what it denies.
findings.whyContradiction: The very next sentence states the conclusion the clause exists to license: *Unde significatur propter diversas operationes, et effectus spiritum Dei DISSIMILITER appellari, cum sit unus atque idem* — "whence it is signified that on account of different operations and effects the spirit of God is DIFFERENTLY NAMED, though he is one and the same." If the same spirit were the spirit of wrath toward Israel as well as toward the Egyptians, there would be no dissimilar naming and no inference to draw. The preceding clause has already fixed the contrast: *Iste itaque spiritus Dei in Aegyptios, nam spiritus irae ejus*.

findings.printedLatin: Quia sterilis, inquit, peperit septem et MULTA IN FILIIS infirmata est.
findings.englishAsRendered: For the barren, he says, hath borne seven, and SHE THAT HAD MANY CHILDREN is made weak.
findings.conjecture: Read "and she that was MANY IN SONS is made weak" — the phrasing Migne prints here and the phrasing our own English uses everywhere else for it.
findings.whyContradiction: This sentence is quoted expressly as the OTHER reading (*In Hebraeo et in Septuaginta translatione non plurimi, sed septem leguntur*), set against the lemma « Donec sterilis peperit plurimos et QUAE MULTOS HABEBAT FILIOS infirmata est ». Our English gives the two Latins the same English words for the second half, so the reader cannot see that they differ; and our English elsewhere renders *multa in filiis* correctly — "her who was many in sons" (1100C, of the earthly Jerusalem), "her that was many in sons" (1101A), "who was many in sons" (chunk 0004, 1102D). Only inside the quoted variant does the Vulgate phrasing reappear.

findings.printedLatin: « Quia non in fortitudine roborabitur vir. » Hoc est, non in fortitudine PROPRIA, sed in virtute divina potens est vir…
findings.englishAsRendered: « For no man shall be strengthened by HIS OWN strength. » That is, not by his own strength but by the divine power is a man mighty…
findings.conjecture: Migne prints the lemma without *sua* (Vulgate 1 Reg. 2:9 has *in fortitudine sua*). Read "For not by strength shall a man be strengthened"; the possessive belongs only to the gloss.
findings.whyContradiction: Rabanus's gloss exists precisely to supply the word the lemma lacks — *Hoc est, non in fortitudine PROPRIA* — and is vacuous if the lemma already said "his own." Our English makes the commentator explain a word he is in fact adding.

findings.printedLatin: « Benigne fac in bona voluntate tua, Sion, ut aedificentur muri Jerusalem. » Ut acceptabile fiat IN EA Domino sacrificium justitiae…
findings.englishAsRendered: « Deal kindly, O Sion, in thy good will, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up. » So that there may be made acceptable IN HER to the Lord the sacrifice of justice…
findings.conjecture: *Sion* is the accusative object, not a vocative: "Deal kindly in thy good will with Sion." Migne drops the Vulgate's *Domine* (Ps. 50:20), which is what makes the vocative reading tempting; the agent is still God.
findings.whyContradiction: Rabanus's own continuation treats Sion as the place acted upon, not the actor — *Ut acceptabile fiat IN EA Domino sacrificium justitiae*, "that in HER the sacrifice of justice may be made acceptable TO THE LORD" — and the whole gloss identifies Sion with the Church, whose walls are built by God's good will, not her own. Our English hands the *bona voluntas* to Sion and leaves no one to build the walls.
